narrative_profile: dark psychological thriller-romance, single first-person POV, surveillance cat-and-mouse, domestic gaslighting, slow-burn romance with explicit consent, no violence, no police procedural, no hacker or tech deus ex machina, evidence-driven climax
title_working: The Things I Let Him See
surface_case: The reader appears to be following Calder Reed, a private surveillance operative hired by Grant Hart to document the deteriorating behavior of Grant's separated wife, Lena. Grant claims Lena has become forgetful, paranoid, and incapable of safely managing the condominium apartment they jointly own. Calder observes Lena from a rented apartment across the condominium's narrow interior courtyard, plus authorized access to selected common-area camera feeds through Grant's position as board president. The apparent story is a dark-romance cat-and-mouse in which the watcher may become either Lena's protector or another man trying to own her reality.
true_case: Grant Hart has spent seven weeks manufacturing a pattern of instability around Lena before Chapter One. Lena detects the surveillance in Chapter Three and begins controlling what Calder can observe. She builds diagnostic tests, each retaining at least one useful outcome even if Calder works entirely for Grant. The certified honeytoken in Chapter Eight confirms mail interception. The final evidence trap forces Grant to commit to a calculated lie that contradicts independent footage. Calder's initial surveillance is a violation and is never retroactively redefined as consent. The romantic and sexual relationship begins only after Lena confronts Calder and sets explicit, revocable terms in Chapter Ten.
core_question: Does Lena want Calder when he is no longer useful as a witness, no longer controls the only evidence, has no contract, no surveillance access, and she can reject him without losing the case?
emotional_question: Can Calder learn to possess the woman directing his gaze without owning her reality, and can Lena trust that his attention is chosen rather than engineered?
book1_promise: Lena defeats Grant's control without being physically rescued and remains in her apartment. Calder gives up sole custody of the evidence, exposes his own conduct to Detective Cross, and accepts Lena's refusal to let him decide for her. After those actions can no longer benefit her case, Lena asks Calder to return without recording equipment; she grants no unrestricted access and chooses when he enters, when he watches, and when the curtain closes.
case_closed: Grant's manipulation is exposed through the false chain of custody trap; the settlement is halted; Grant loses admin access; the evidence enters official custody for investigation. Lena retains possession of the apartment.
series_door_opened: Mae gives Lena a sealed archived complaint from another condominium that used the same security vendor. The complaint predates Grant's board position and describes short camera gaps paired with resident instability reports. Lena does not open it during Book One. The hook offers a future choice: leave the surveillance world behind, or examine whether the mechanism existed before Grant learned to exploit it.
book2_hook: Mae gives Lena a sealed archived complaint from another condominium that used the same security vendor. The complaint predates Grant's board position and describes short camera gaps paired with resident instability reports. Lena does not open it during Book One. Grant remains defeated and does not secretly control the new problem; no replacement antagonist appears on-page.
book1_ending_type: hopeful resolution with romantic payoff after all dependencies end
reader_payoff_book1: The thriller question is resolved: Lena, not Calder or Grant, controlled the decisive sequence of visible events. The romance question is answered: Lena chooses Calder only after she no longer needs him, and he accepts her terms. The emotional payoff is chosen visibility rather than enforced observation.
